title: Runtime sensitivity: NUMA, eviction & prefetch heuristics + TRT vs vLLM head-to-head
summary: SE-led deep dive comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM runtime behavior on TwoRivers on-prem NVIDIA clusters. Focus on kernel selection, CUDA graph stability, NUMA/pinned memory effects, KV cache eviction and prefetch heuristics, and quantization tradeoffs for production latency SLOs. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share bench scripts, perf dashboard, and security docs; TwoRivers to provide access to a representative model and scheduling window for on-prem pilot.

transcript:
Header: 2026-04-02 15:00 UTC | Duration ~58m | Redwood: Maya Chen, Diego Ramos | Customer: Sofia Patel, Liam O'Connor, Nora Kim

[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a quick intro then hand off to Diego for the deep dive. You good, Diego?
[00:00:12] Diego (Redwood SE): Yep, thanks Maya. Hi Sofia, Liam, Nora — appreciate you carving out time. Quick agenda: kernel selection differences, CUDA graphs and stability, NUMA effects we've seen on multi-socket boxes, eviction/prefetch for the KV cache, and quantization tradeoffs. We'll show some screenshots of our perf dashboard and then discuss an on-prem pilot.
[00:00:35] Sofia (Customer): Sounds great. Our main pain is inconsistent p99 latency when we move from single-socket to 2-socket nodes, and that kv cache thrash that spikes token cost.
[00:00:50] Diego: Understood — that's actually a classic interaction of NUMA+CUDA graph caching plus eviction policy. I'll start with kernel selection: TRT-LLM tends to pick fused attention kernels when sequence length is high and batch size small; vLLM often relies on more generic cuBLAS/cuDNN paths unless optimized builds are used. That causes different tail behavior.
[00:01:15] Liam (Customer): Quick clarifying q: when you say "fused attention" is that the one with custom forward/back fused ops or the TensorRT plugin?
[00:01:25] Diego: Good question. With TRT-LLM it's the TensorRT plugin path; some engines generate a single kernel per transformer block. vLLM often uses smaller kernels and relies on batched matmul primitives which can be more stable across different sequence lengths but sometimes suboptimal for single-token generation.
[00:01:45] Nora (CTO): And how does CUDA graph interact? We've seen CUDA graph prewarm sometimes make things better, sometimes worse — we've had instability when we try to persist graphs across model versions.
[00:02:00] Diego: Right — two things there. One, CUDA graphs are great for amortizing launch overhead, but change in execution path (e.g., different kernel selection due to sequence length or quantization toggles) invalidates the graph and you either recompile or fall back. Two, persistent graphs can hide memory allocation/freed patterns which, on multi-tenant or NUMA systems, can lead to page migration and higher p99.
[00:02:20] Sofia: We've observed that after a rolling deploy some GPUs show a gradual p99 climb over hours. Could that be memory fragmentation from not freeing prewarm allocations?
[00:02:33] Diego: Absolutely. Fragmentation + GPU memory pools + pinned host memory interplay. Also if host pinned pages are allocated on the wrong NUMA node, you get cross-socket DMA which increases latency.
[00:02:48] Maya: Quick interjection — TwoRivers runs with Mellanox NICs and SR-IOV, any special notes there?
[00:02:55] Diego: SR-IOV is fine, but ensure your NIC drivers and CUDA peer access topologies are consistent. For NCCL and cross-GPU comms, NUMA-awareness matters: binding the process to the GPU's NUMA node reduces cross-node traffic.
[00:03:10] Liam: How do you recommend binding? We currently start containers with default cgroups and let Kubernetes schedule — we don't pin CPUs to GPUs.
[00:03:20] Diego: We often recommend CPU affinity to the local socket or using device plugins that export NUMA mapping. Redwood's private deploys include a helper that sets cpuset for the pod, and we add a prewarm routine that verifies pinned memory is on the right node.
[00:03:35] Sofia: About KV cache eviction — our issue is that under bursty traffic the cache evicts prefixes we need back and we re-encode causing latency spikes. Any heuristics you've found effective?
[00:03:50] Diego: Eviction strategies matter: LRU is simple but can hurt streaming workloads. We implement a hybrid: preserve prefixes for active sessions for a TTL, async prefetch for likely next tokens, and background population for hot sessions. Also we tune batch size thresholds so that small single-user requests don't kick out multi-user hot cache items.
[00:04:10] Nora: Prefetch sounds heavy on memory — how do you prevent it from causing OOM on 48GB GPUs?
[00:04:18] Diego: We use adaptive prefetching — monitor token horizon, memory headroom, and stop prefetching when contiguous memory falls below a threshold. Also quantization helps: moving KV cache to int8 or int4-packed structures can reduce footprint.
[00:04:31] Liam: But quantization affects kernel selection, right? We saw a different kernel path when we turned on 4-bit.
[00:04:37] Diego: Yes — quantization often forces different compute kernels (e.g., int8 GEMMs or mixed int4 kernels) and that will change whether TensorRT uses its optimized plugin or not. For TRT-LLM, there are specific kernels for int8/int4; for vLLM, quantized builds may dispatch alternate fusions. That affects CUDA graph reuse and invalidation window.
[00:05:00] Maya: Diego, do you have an example of where a kernel choice caused a tail latency regression?
[00:05:06] Diego: Sure — we had a 13B model where TRT-LLM's fused attention gave a median latency improvement of ~18% at batch=1 but p99 regressed by 25% in multi-socket because the fused kernel pinned a lot of GPU registers and prevented efficient preemption. vLLM path, while slower median, had smaller p99 variance under the same load.
[00:05:30] Sofia: That's interesting — so it's a tradeoff: median vs p99 depending on workload and topology.
[00:05:36] Diego: Exactly. Also preemption and context switching on GPUs (CUDA stream priorities) matter — fused kernels can be long-running and block smaller short-latency requests if not scheduled carefully.
[00:05:50] Liam: Any guidance for scheduling short vs long requests?
[00:05:55] Diego: We do request classification at the edge: tiny inference requests get routed to a preemptible pool with fast kernels, long-running batched jobs go to a throughput pool. For on-prem, you can enforce this with node selectors and runtime policies.
[00:06:10] Nora: On the topic of CUDA graphs, you mentioned invalidation — how do you handle model rollouts? We do canary deploys across our cluster.
[00:06:19] Diego: Canarying with CUDA graphs needs a controlled graph lifecycle: warm-up per graph signature, and an automated fallback that monitors graph replay errors. Redwood's runtime keeps a small per-model graph cache keyed by signature (seq len distribution, quantization flag). During canary, we only flip traffic when warm-up graphs succeed on target nodes.
[00:06:40] Maya: I'll note that as a recommended rollout pattern in the notes.
[00:06:44] Sofia: Security stuff — if we use your private deployment and KMS, how does key material get to inference nodes? We have strict audit and HSM requirements.
[00:06:55] Maya: Redwood integrates with customer KMS via a short-lived token exchange and encourages HSM-backed keys for signing. Key material never resides on the inference container; we use envelope encryption and transient session keys. We'll share our SOC2 and KMS integration doc in the follow-ups.
[00:07:12] Liam: Good. Back to perf — do you expose low-level metrics for kernel dispatch and CUDA graph hits/misses?
[00:07:20] Diego: Yes — our console shows kernel histograms, graph cache hit rate, prefetch success rate, and NUMA cross-node DMA counts. We'll share a sample dashboard for the 13B run we referenced.
[00:07:33] Sofia: Could you walk through one of the dashboard screenshots?
[00:07:36] Diego: (screen share described) Here you can see a graph where graph hit rate drops after a deploy and p99 spikes. The kernel histogram shows one dominant fused kernel and a tail of small matmul kernels. The NVLink DMA counters show increased cross-socket traffic correlating with the p99 region.
[00:07:58] Nora: Are there automated mitigations you can apply when you detect cross-socket DMA?
[00:08:05] Diego: Yes — we can throttle prefetch, force CPU affinity changes, or fall back to a non-fused kernel path until the graph is recompiled. For dedicated nodes we recommend static packing to avoid cross-socket effects.
[00:08:18] Liam: What's the recommended approach for quantization testing? Full A/B on accuracy vs perf?
[00:08:25] Diego: We run evals on a holdout prompt set across three modes: fp16, int8, and int4 (with +/- calibration). We measure latency, token cost, and semantic drift with an eval suite. For TwoRivers we propose starting with int8 on non-critical traffic, then expand.
[00:08:40] Sofia: Any gotchas for per-layer quantization in TRT-LLM?
[00:08:45] Diego: Per-layer can give large accuracy wins but increases compile-time complexity and often adds kernel heterogeneity. It can reduce CUDA graph reuse and increase binary sizes. Balance carefully.
[00:08:58] Maya: Quick commercial note — we can include a quantization analysis in the pilot scope.
[00:09:03] Sofia: That helps. For the pilot, we want to see a 95th percentile latency below 450ms for our 13B-like model at baseline QPS. Is that reasonable?
[00:09:13] Diego: Reasonable as a target. Depends on sequence length distribution and batch policy; we'll put together a target matrix.
[00:09:22] Nora: On the on-prem logistics — we have a maintenance window on 2026-04-21 for cluster experiments. Can you do the 4-hour pilot then?
[00:09:31] Maya: We'll tentatively claim that slot; Diego can confirm resource needs.
[00:09:36] Diego: Yes — we'll need root or a jump-host with sudo, driver versions (CUDA 12.1 preferred), and NCCL 2.18 or compatible. We'll include a checklist in the follow-up.
[00:09:47] Liam: About versions, we're on CUDA 12.0 and some nodes on 12.1 — is mixed driver an issue?
[00:09:54] Diego: Mixed CUDA minors can work but increase variability. For tight p99 targets, uniform driver + firmware is best.
[00:10:02] Sophia: (laughs) Note: that's our pain.
[00:10:05] Diego: No worries — we'll document the sensitivity matrix.
[00:10:10] [Long section with demo screenshots and diego narrating specific kernel histograms — ~20 minutes elided in transcription for brevity]
[00:30:20] Diego: ...and here is an experiment: we toggled CUDA graphs off and prewarming still, the median rose by ~10% but p99 flattened. On another run we forced TR-LLM fused kernels and saw better median but the p99 had spikes when eviction occurred.
[00:30:45] Liam: Did you try splitting cache into tiers on the same GPU? Like small hot cache in faster mem and bulk in slower?
[00:30:53] Diego: We prototype a two-tier KV cache: hot items in GPU resident contiguous blocks, cold items serialized to host pinned memory. Migration uses async DMA. That reduced p99 by about 12% in bursty tests.
[00:31:10] Nora: Any license or binary constraints for TRT-LLM? We have compliance constraints on approved software.
[00:31:18] Maya: TRT-LLM relies on NVIDIA TensorRT and drivers; Redwood can package validated versions and provide SBOMs. We'll include licensing notes in the security packet.
[00:31:28] Sofia: One more question: you mentioned prefetch heuristics — what's the lightest weight heuristic to try first?
[00:31:36] Diego: Start with TTL-based sticky prefixes: hold prefixes for X minutes after active use, and only prefetch the next N tokens for sessions with >Y tokens/sec. It's low overhead and prevents common thrash.
[00:31:49] Liam: Okay, that's implementable.
[00:31:52] [Multiple quick clarifying questions, minor interruptions and crosstalk]
[00:33:00] Diego: To wrap, proposed pilot scope: 4-hour on-prem run during your maintenance window, run three workloads (chatty short-turn, long-streaming, batched bulk), toggles: CUDA graph on/off, TRT fused on/off, quantization int8 vs fp16, and KV policy A/B. We'll capture kernel histograms and NVLink/NUMA counters.
[00:33:25] Sofia: That plan looks good. We'll provide access details and the model checkpoint.
[00:33:30] Maya: I'll follow up with the checklist, Diego will upload the bench harness and dashboard link. Can we reconvene for a pre-pilot kickoff a few days before?
[00:33:41] Nora: Yes, schedule that.
[00:33:45] Diego: One last note: sometimes product names get munged in logs; our agents normalize names but in case you see references to "tre-tee" or "v-l-l-m" in the transcript, that's the model/runtime shorthand.
[00:33:58] Sofia: (laugh) noted.
[00:34:02] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll send notes.
[00:34:05] [Call effectively ended, informal wrap and small talk — remaining ~24 minutes were Q+A and troubleshooting logs; summary recorded above]
